## From Designed Teams to Optimized Coordination

The same artifacts that make coordination auditable also make it optimizable. Once systems record messages, costs, verifier outcomes, memory updates, tool calls, and artifact diffs, coordination is no longer only a design choice. It becomes a policy over allocation: who acts, what they see, when they communicate, which artifact enters shared state, when to stop, and when to escalate.

This is a distinct historical turn:

```text
hand-written roles -> programmable workflows -> measured mechanisms -> optimized coordination
```

One family optimizes the graph of collaboration. DyLAN models collaboration as a dynamic temporal network, selecting task-relevant agents and pruning active participants through team optimization, ranking, and early stopping [@dylan]. GPTSwarm represents language agents as optimizable computational graphs and uses edge optimization to learn communication distributions, including settings where harmful agents must be filtered from the graph [@gptswarm]. AgentNet moves toward decentralized routing: local routers decide whether to forward, split, or execute tasks, while local memory and edge updates support specialization without fixed roles [@agentnet]. These systems treat communication edges, team size, active membership, and routing as variables to learn or select, not as constants chosen by the designer.

Another family optimizes the workflow or controller. MaAS introduces a query-dependent agentic supernet over operators such as CoT, Debate, Self-Refine, ReAct, Ensemble, Self-Consistency, Testing, and early exit, reporting competitive performance at 6-45% of the inference cost of several handcrafted or automated alternatives in its setup [@maas]. OMAC frames multi-agent collaboration as information flow over a graph and optimizes functional and structural dimensions, including agent prompts, new-agent construction, candidate-team selection, dynamic participation, and communication routing [@omac]. @evolvingorchestration train a centralized policy to activate agents from a fixed pool while optimizing task reward and token cost, showing improved average performance and declining token use in the reported settings. MAS-GPT moves architecture construction into a learned generator: given a query, a fine-tuned model emits an executable Python `forward` function defining agent prompts, calls, and information flow [@masgpt]. These systems make the collaboration structure itself a candidate artifact: searched, sampled, generated, evaluated, and reused.

The strongest conceptual shift comes when the interacting agents themselves are trained for collaboration. ACC-Collab treats collaboration as learned actor-critic behavior rather than an emergent property of prompted deliberation [@acccollab]. It alternates training an actor that answers and a critic that gives feedback, using guided collaborative trajectories and preference optimization to improve multi-round deliberation on QA-style benchmarks. MAPoRL makes the point even more directly: it treats collaborative debate as a multi-agent reinforcement learning problem in which agents are co-trained with verifier-based rewards, including incentives for useful self-revision and influence on later answers [@maporl]. Its no-collaboration control helps separate learned interaction behavior from ordinary task-knowledge gains, and its transfer experiments suggest that some collaboration behavior can generalize across the tested datasets.

| Approach | Optimized object | Feedback signal | Main evidence | Main caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DyLAN, GPTSwarm, AgentNet | Team membership, communication edges, routing, and local specialization | Task reward, peer ranking, graph utility, or evolved edge weights | Smaller or optimized teams can outperform larger fixed teams; harmful or weak edges can be pruned | Benefits are benchmark- and pool-dependent, and optimization cost or transfer may be undercounted |
| MaAS, OMAC, evolving orchestration | Query-dependent workflows, operators, controller policies, depth, width, and stopping | Supervised task performance, task reward, token cost, or contrastive positive-negative comparisons | Adaptive systems can improve average performance while reducing inference cost in reported settings | Training/search cost, reward design, and cross-domain robustness remain central concerns |
| MAS-GPT | Executable MAS code generated from the query | Selected and refined query-MAS training pairs | Per-query MAS construction can be moved into one generator inference | Generated structures do not by themselves solve tool integration, memory governance, safety, or runtime reliability |
| ACC-Collab, MAPoRL | Critic behavior, revision policy, influence, and collaborative debate behavior | Known answers, preference pairs, learned verifiers, and multi-agent rewards | Trained agents revise and critique more usefully than prompted off-the-shelf debate in tested settings | Evidence is mostly short-horizon QA or debate with automatic verifiers and reward-hacking risk |

: Coordination-optimization approaches grouped by the object being learned or searched. Current methods optimize collaboration graphs, query-dependent workflows, generated MAS code, or the agents' own critique and revision behavior, with different feedback signals and transfer risks. {#tbl-coordination-optimization}

The optimization turn directly addresses a missing assumption in early multi-agent LLM work. If off-the-shelf agents do not naturally model partners, revise appropriately, disagree usefully, preserve commitments, or route information well, prompting alone may not be enough. Coordination can become a trainable object: critic behavior, revision policy, routing policy, communication graph, stopping rule, and even MAS-construction policy can all be optimized.

The caveat is important. Current coordination-optimization evidence is promising but narrower than the artifact and evaluation evidence. Many results use QA, math, coding-function, or controlled reasoning benchmarks; many rely on automatic verifiers; and many evaluate fixed agent pools or short interaction horizons. A mature claim should test transfer across task families, model backbones, tool environments, and artifact-heavy workflows. It should report optimization cost, inference cost, latency, robustness, reward hacking, and failure modes. Learned orchestration should also be evaluated against the same standards as handcrafted teams: budget-matched single agents, sampling baselines, workflow baselines, artifact degradation, shared-state safety, and human review cost.

The lesson is not that optimized coordination replaces artifacts, verification, or human review. It is that those mechanisms provide the feedback substrate for allocation. The mature question is therefore a control question: when should the system spend compute on serial reasoning, parallel search, routing, debate, artifact verification, memory repair, human escalation, or stopping?
